answer: SES (socioeconomic status) is the variable. Its logit coefficient on BA DEGREE COMPLETED drops from a positive +0.36/+0.47 to −0.23 once SAMPLE_RACE and the academic variables (ABILITY composite + PERCENTILE IN CLASS) are added, a classic suppression pattern.

payload.hypothesis: Socioeconomic status (SES) is the variable whose effect on BA degree completion reverses. In a bivariate logit, higher SES predicts degree completion (coefficient ≈ +0.36 on a unit-variance scale, ≈ +0.47 raw, p<.001). Once race and academic characteristics (ability test composite and class percentile) are added, the SES coefficient flips to ≈ −0.23 and its significance is lost — a suppression pattern indicating SES mainly captures race/ability-related advantage that is directly modeled by the controls, leaving only a small negative residual association.
payload.workflow: Loaded nls_ses_processed.csv (8773 rows, 0 missing). Ran logit (primary) and OLS/LPM (robustness) regressions of BA DEGREE COMPLETED on each candidate (SES, FAMILY SIZE, SEX) as Model A, then adding race dummies (White ref) + ABILITY + PERCENTILE as Model B, reporting coef/SE/z/p/95%CI. Investigated the A-coefficient gap via unit-variance standardization of SES. Characterized the flip as suppression using pairwise correlations and Model B VIFs.
